text: Why do I get butterflies when I'm nervous?

steps.title: The alarm goes off
steps.say: This is an example nervous moment. Your brain's threat centre fires, and a nerve pathway, the sympathetic system, sends a 'get ready' signal down your spine to every organ.

composed.caption: Threat signal leaves the brain
composed.basis: Textbook fight-or-flight response (Cannon; standard physiology texts)

steps.title: Heart speeds up, gut loses blood
steps.say: Adrenaline pushes your heart from about 78 to about 91 beats a minute and squeezes the gut's vessels, so blood shifts toward muscles you might need to run.

steps.title: Digestion is put on hold
steps.say: With less blood and a 'not now' signal, your stomach slows, so your pizza leaves it noticeably slower. Digestion isn't a priority when you might be in danger.

steps.title: Where the flutter comes from
steps.say: Your gut has its own dense nerve network. Narrowed vessels and stalled, twitchy muscle make those nerves fire, and the vagus nerve carries that odd sensation up to your brain.

composed.caption: Gut nerves report the squeeze upward
composed.basis: Gut-brain axis and enteric nervous system (Mayer, Nat Rev Neurosci 2011); about 80% of vagus fibres carry signals upward

steps.title: It settles once the moment passes
steps.say: About an hour after the nerves fade, your heart is back near 78 and blood pressure is back to normal. The flutter fades with them as adrenaline is cleared.

lines.text: When you're nervous, your brain sets off its fight-or-flight alarm. That moves blood away from your gut.
Your stomach slows, its nerves fire, and the vagus nerve carries that flutter up to your brain.
You may feel it fade within an hour or so as the adrenaline clears.
